title: Numbers every programmer should know
objectives: Order the costs of a register, cache, memory, disk and network access by powers of ten.

screens.title: Fastest to slowest
screens.prose: An interviewer opens with a warm-up. No numbers yet: just your sense of the machine and the network.
screens.question: Order these from fastest to slowest.

lines.text: A random read from an NVMe solid-state drive
A seek on a spinning disk
A London to New York round trip

hints.text: Which of these has to cross an ocean?
Chips inside the core beat memory chips, and memory beats any drive.
Register, L1, DRAM, NVMe, disk seek, then London to New York.

feedback.correct: That's it. The six span more than eight powers of ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with what sits inside the core, and end with the ocean.

byKey.dram: Main memory sits outside the core, so the L1 cache comes before it.
byKey.nvme: An NVMe drive is fast storage, but still slower than any memory chip.
byKey.seek: A seek moves a metal arm across a platter, which takes milliseconds.
byKey.ny: A London to New York trip is fixed by the speed of light over 5,570 km.

explain.text: Register 0.3 ns, L1 1 ns, DRAM 100 ns, NVMe 100 µs. Then a disk seek 10 ms and London to New York 60 ms: round figures for a desktop core. Know each to a power of ten, not to the digit.

screens.title: One power of ten per step
screens.prose: The six accesses sit on a log scale, where each power of ten is the same width. Slide the marker from the L1 read to the disk seek.

derive.caption: The marker is {{round(log10(probe.x))}} powers of ten from 1 ns, an L1 read.

screens.question: How many powers of ten separate an L1 read from a disk seek?

hints.text: Read the marker caption at the disk seek.
The disk seek sits at 10 ms, which is $10^7$ ns.

feedback.correct: Seven: 1 ns to 10 ms is ten million times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the powers of ten, not the gaps between labels.

byKey.ratio: 10,000,000 is the ratio itself. The question asks for its power of ten.
byKey.six: You may have counted the steps from 10 ns. Start at 1 ns, where the L1 read sits.

explain.text: From 1 ns to 10 ms is $10^7$: seven equal steps on this scale. We call this list the **latency ladder**. Each rung is a power of ten you should know.

screens.title: If a nanosecond were a second
screens.prose: Stretch time so that 1 ns lasts one second. An L1 read then takes a second. For depth, the free long paper *What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory* covers this level.

state.caption: Stretch: 1 ns of real time becomes 1 s.

screens.question: Fill in the human time of each access, in seconds.

hints.text: Write each real time in nanoseconds first.
1 µs is 1,000 ns and 1 ms is 1,000,000 ns.

feedback.correct: That's it. A main-memory read is a minute and 40 seconds; a disk seek is months.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert each time to nanoseconds; each one becomes that many seconds.

byKey.r1c2: 100 ns becomes 100 s at one second per nanosecond.

explain.text: An NVMe read becomes 100,000 s, which is 1 day 3 h 46 min 40 s. A disk seek becomes 115.7 days. London to New York becomes 694.4 days, about 1.9 years.

screens.title: A time budget
screens.prose: A feed handler receives 200,000 messages a second, and one core handles them all. So each message gets $1\text{ s} / 200{,}000 = 5$ µs.

state.caption: One message gets 5 µs of one core.

screens.question: How many main-memory reads fit in that budget?

hints.text: Write 5 µs in nanoseconds.
5 µs is 5,000 ns, and a main-memory read is 100 ns.

feedback.correct: 50 reads. Fifty cache misses use the whole budget.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the budget in ns by the cost of one read.

byKey.l1: 5,000 is the count of L1 reads. A main-memory read costs 100 ns, not 1 ns.
byKey.us: 5 is the budget in microseconds. Divide it by the cost of a read.
byKey.half: Check the zeros: 5,000 ns / 100 ns is 50.

explain.text: 5 µs is 5,000 ns, and $5{,}000 / 100 = 50$. The same budget holds 5,000 L1 reads. A handler that misses the cache fifty times a message cannot keep up.

screens.title: Light sets a floor
screens.prose: No signal beats light. A trading firm in London wants the fastest path to Frankfurt.

rows: London to New York, straight line

state.caption: A round trip covers the distance twice.

screens.question: Work out the round trips, in milliseconds.

hints.text: A round trip is 1,280 km.
Time is distance over speed: 1,280 / 200,000 s.
6.4 ms in fibre, 4.27 ms in air, so 2.13 ms saved.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the distance, divide by the speed, then turn seconds into ms.

byKey.r0c1: Use 1,280 km at 200,000 km/s. If you got 3.2 ms, that is one way.
byKey.r1c1: Use 1,280 km at 299,792 km/s. Double the 640 km first.

explain.text: Fibre: $1{,}280 / 200{,}000$ s is 6.4 ms. Through air: $1{,}280 / 299{,}792$ s is 4.27 ms, which saves 2.13 ms. That saving is why firms pay for microwave links between cities.

screens.title: Neighbours on the ladder
screens.prose: The interviewer points at two neighbours on the ladder.

state.caption: DRAM at 100 ns, NVMe at 100 µs.

screens.question: An NVMe read against a main-memory read: how many times slower?

options.why: You compared 100 µs with 100 ns and dropped the units. A µs is 1,000 ns.
That is DRAM against an L1 read.
That is NVMe against an L1 read.

hints.text: Put both in nanoseconds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the two figures; do not count rungs.

byKey.b: You dropped the units. 100 µs is 100,000 ns, so the ratio is $10^3$.
byKey.c: 100 times is the gap from L1 up to DRAM.

explain.text: $100{,}000 / 100 = 1{,}000$. Neighbours on the ladder can be one, two or three powers of ten apart. Divide the figures; never count rungs.

screens.title: The floor and the figure
screens.prose: Our round figure for London to New York is 60 ms. Physics gives a floor below it.

rows: London to New York, straight line

state.caption: A round trip covers the distance twice.

screens.question: What is the fibre floor on a London to New York round trip, in ms?

hints.text: A round trip is twice 5,570 km.

feedback.correct: 55.7 ms, just under the 60 ms figure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the distance and use the fibre speed.

byKey.oneway: 27.85 ms is one way. Double it for the round trip.
byKey.air: 37.16 ms is the floor through air. The cable is glass.
byKey.sixty: 60 ms is the round figure. The floor is what physics alone allows.

explain.text: $11{,}140 / 200{,}000$ s is 55.7 ms. Cables do not run in straight lines, so real trips sit above the floor. Physics sets a floor; every real route only adds to it.

screens.title: One division
screens.prose:
Every answer today was one division:

$$n = \frac{\text{budget}}{\text{cost per access}}$$

| Access | Round figure |
|---|---:|
| Register | 0.3 ns |
| L1 | 1 ns |
| L2 | 4 ns |
| L3 | 20 ns |
| DRAM | 100 ns |
| NVMe read | 100 µs |
| Same-data-centre round trip | 500 µs |
| Disk seek | 10 ms |
| London to New York | 60 ms |
screens.question: A 2 µs budget: how many L3 reads fit?

options.why: You left the budget in µs: 2 / 20. In nanoseconds it is 2,000 / 20.
You used the L1 figure of 1 ns.
You used the main-memory figure of 100 ns.

hints.text: 2 µs is 2,000 ns.
An L3 read is 20 ns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 2,000 ns by the L3 figure.

explain.text: $2{,}000 / 20 = 100$. The method never changes: budget in nanoseconds over cost in nanoseconds.

screens.title: Drill: budgets
screens.prose: Drill: about 90 seconds each. Say the reasoning aloud first, then type the number. Use the round figures.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: Powers of ten from an L1 read to an NVMe read
NVMe reads in one disk seek

hints.text: Write every time in nanoseconds.
A same-data-centre round trip is 500 µs, which is 500,000 ns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: Each is a budget over a cost, in the same unit. The powers-of-ten question is the same division, read as an exponent. In an interview, say the units aloud as you divide.

screens.title: Follow-up: a price from New York
screens.prose: The interviewer extends the edge case. A London strategy trades on a price set in New York.

rows: London to New York, straight line

state.caption: A round trip covers the distance twice.

screens.question: What is the least time before that price can reach London, in ms?

hints.text: The price only travels one way.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One way, at the fibre speed.

byKey.rtt: 55.7 ms is a round trip. The price only has to arrive.
byKey.air: 18.58 ms is through air. The question asks about fibre.
byKey.round: 30 ms is half the round figure. Use the floor: distance over speed.

explain.text: $5{,}570 / 200{,}000$ s is 27.85 ms. Nothing the London desk does can shorten it.

screens.title: Follow-up: react or predict
screens.prose: A desk in New York sees that price the moment it is set. Ours sees it 27.85 ms later.

rows: London to New York, straight line

state.caption: A round trip covers the distance twice.

screens.question: Can the London strategy ever react to that price first?

options.text: No. It can predict the price, but never react first.
Yes, with a faster server and network card in London.
options.why: You treated it as a computing problem. The delay is in the cable.

options.text: Yes, over a microwave link instead of a cable.
options.why: Air cuts the trip to about 18.6 ms, but New York still sees the price first.

options.text: Yes, if the price is sent over UDP, not TCP.
options.why: A protocol changes overhead, not the speed of light.

hints.text: Where is the price set?
Any path from New York takes at least the floor.
Only a prediction can beat a signal that has not arrived.

feedback.correct: No. London can only predict it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether anything in London can shorten the trip.

byKey.b: A faster server saves microseconds. The trip is 27.85 ms of physics.
byKey.c: Microwave is faster than fibre, but it still starts in New York.

explain.text: No path from New York arrives before light does. A London strategy can model the price, but it cannot react first. Firms buy shorter paths and faster media because that floor is the whole game.

ideas: Know costs to a power of ten: L1 1 ns, DRAM 100 ns, NVMe 100 µs, disk 10 ms.
To count how many accesses fit, divide the time budget by the cost of one access.
Light in fibre covers about 200,000 km a second, so distance sets a floor no code can beat.

formula.name: Accesses in a budget
formula.note: 5 µs over 100 ns is 50 main-memory reads.

summary.trap: Counting rungs instead of dividing: an NVMe read is 1,000 main-memory reads, not 10.

quiz.question: How many L2 reads fit in 1 µs?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 1,000 ns by 4 ns.

byKey.l1: 1,000 is the L1 count. An L2 read costs 4 ns.
byKey.dram: 10 is the main-memory count at 100 ns.

quiz.prose: London to Frankfurt is 640 km in a straight line. Light in fibre covers about 200,000 km/s.
quiz.question: What is the least one-way time in fibre, in ms?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One way is the distance over the speed.

byKey.rtt: 6.4 ms is the round trip. The question is one way.
byKey.air: 2.13 ms is the saving from air, not a trip.

options.why: 10,000 × 1 ns is 10 µs, a tenth of an NVMe read.
500 × 100 ns is 50 µs, half an NVMe read.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each count by its cost.

explain.text: 10 µs, 50 µs and 4 µs all sit below the 100 µs of one NVMe read. Thousands of fast accesses can still cost less than one slow one.

quiz.prose: A vendor offers a London to Frankfurt fibre link with a 5 ms round trip.
quiz.question: Is that possible?

options.text: No: the fibre floor is 6.4 ms.
Yes: fibre carries light, and light is fast enough.
options.why: Light in glass covers about 200,000 km/s, not 299,792 km/s.

options.text: Yes, if the cable runs in a straight line.
options.why: 6.4 ms already assumes a straight line.

options.text: Only with a faster server at each end.
options.why: Servers add time. They cannot remove the time in the cable.

feedback.correct: No. 1,280 km of fibre takes at least 6.4 ms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the floor first.

explain.text: A round trip is 1,280 km, and $1{,}280 / 200{,}000$ s is 6.4 ms. Any fibre link is slower than that. Only a path through air can go below it.
